newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour party disciplines MPs after bribe claims.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour party disciplines MPs after bribe claims.

text.p: The ruling Labour party, keen to show it intends to be tough on any allegations of sleaze, on Wednesday suspended two of its members of parliament from holding any office in the party.

Labour's National Executive Committee (NEC) imposed the sanction on Mohammed Sarwar after allegations he gave money to an election rival and on Robert Wareing after he was reported to have failed to declare a business interest.

Sarwar was later suspended from the privileges of membership of the parliamentary party, meaning he will not be allowed to attend its meetings or represent it on parliamentary committees. A similar sanction was imposed on Wareing last week. Labour, swept to power in a May 1 election landslide, has signalled it will not tolerate any sleaze in its ranks.

Former prime minister John Major was dogged by sleaze in his last years with more than a dozen ministers and aides forced to quit over scandals ranging from sexual affairs to allegations they were paid to ask parliamentary questions.
In most cases Major backed the ministers until the moment they quit, landing him with a reputation as a weak and ineffectual leader at the head of a sleaze-ridden party.

Labour, determined not to fall into the same trap, has beefed up its disciplinary code, allowing it to take action against an MP for anything which contravenes the broad definition of "conduct detrimental to the party".

A suspended MP still receives his salary and is expected to vote with Labour in parliament. The sanction is a form of internal exile. The NEC sanction means the MPs cannot sit on the party's regional executive bodies.

Both MPs maintain their innocence. Sarwar, being investigated by police over allegations he gave an election rival in his Scottish constituency 5,000 pounds ($8,289) not to campaign hard against him, has insisted he will clear his name.
Wareing, suspended for failing to declare a link with a firm reported to be in Serbia, says he has done nothing wrong.
Labour has referred allegations against Wareing and Sarwar to the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner, Sir Gordon Downey, a watchdog appointed by Major to defuse the sleaze crisis.
Labour will complete its own inquiries after Downey finishes his investigation into Wareing and the police complete their investigation into Sarwar, who is Britain's first Moslem MP.
But both would be expected to resign their seats if they were found to have breached the law or parliamentary rules.
Their departure would not cause Prime Minister Tony Blair a problem. His majority currently stands at 179.
